debt.scale.source: IMF, Fiscal Monitor April 2026: Fiscal Policy under Pressure: High Debt, Rising Risks
debt.scale.note: The IMF estimates global government debt at 93.9% of GDP in 2025. Exposure across major sovereign issuers supports a large potential fiscal and financial shock. Debt is also an asset and can finance productive activity; the severity judgment concerns disorderly distress and constrained responses, not indebtedness by itself.

debt.urgency.note: World Bank data show record external-debt interest payments of USD415.4 billion by low- and middle-income countries in 2024. Servicing pressure and constrained financing create immediate policy needs. The range allows for differing maturities, currencies and market access; this burden does not establish that every borrower faces imminent default.

debt.acceleration.source: IMF, Fiscal Monitor April 2026: Fiscal Policy under Pressure: High Debt, Rising Risks
debt.acceleration.note: IMF estimates put global public debt at 92.0% of GDP in 2024 and 93.9% in 2025, while advanced economies excluding the United States declined slightly. The central score therefore reflects moderate aggregate worsening with heterogeneous country paths, not an across-the-board debt explosion. Preliminary estimates remain revisable.

debt.interdependence.source: IMF, Global Financial Stability Report April 2026: Global Financial Markets Confront the War in the Middle East and Amplification Risks
debt.interdependence.note: The IMF identifies a sovereign-bank feedback channel, refinancing pressures and leveraged nonbank amplification. These mechanisms connect debt distress to credit, public services and external financing. The high central judgment reflects several coupled sectors, while the lower bound allows orderly refinancing and policy support to interrupt transmission.

debt.irreversibility.note: The World Bank documents debt-service and financing burdens that can displace investment and development spending. Such losses may persist through human-capital and infrastructure effects. Debt contracts can nevertheless be restructured and fiscal positions can improve, so irreversibility is scored materially below ecological or nuclear damage; persistence depends on crisis management.

debt.gov_failure.source: IMF, Fiscal Monitor April 2026: Fiscal Policy under Pressure: High Debt, Rising Risks
debt.gov_failure.note: The IMF describes competing spending demands and higher interest burdens, making credible adjustment harder. This supports a substantial risk of delayed or inadequate responses, but available fiscal tools and creditor coordination prevent an automatic extreme rating. The range reflects political capacity, monetary sovereignty and differences among borrowers.

debt.growth_rate.source: IMF, Fiscal Monitor April 2026: Fiscal Policy under Pressure: High Debt, Rising Risks
debt.growth_rate.note: IMF estimates show world government debt rising from 92.0% to 93.9% of GDP during 2025, about 2.07% relative indicator growth. This provides a modest pressure proxy after conversion. The preliminary global ratio conceals declining country groups, and neither debt quantity nor this growth rate directly measures default likelihood.

displacement.scale.source: UNHCR South Africa, World Refugee Day 2026: solidarity and solutions
displacement.scale.note: UNHCR reports 117.8 million forcibly displaced people at end-2025. This is major humanitarian exposure across regions, supporting substantial potential harm through lost livelihoods, protection gaps and stressed services. The threat is forced displacement and inadequate protection; the judgment does not treat displaced people themselves as a destabilizing cause.

displacement.urgency.source: UNHCR South Africa, World Refugee Day 2026: solidarity and solutions
displacement.urgency.note: UNHCR emphasizes access to services, livelihoods and durable solutions alongside historically high displacement. Existing unmet needs warrant urgent action within the current decade. The upper range captures prolonged exclusion, while inclusion and effective local support can reduce pressure; the score is a humanitarian-priority judgment, not a migration forecast.

displacement.acceleration.source: UNRIC, July 2026 library newsletter: Global Trends, Forced Displacement in 2025
displacement.acceleration.note: The UN summary of Global Trends 2025 reports the first decline in global forced displacement in a decade, alongside substantial returns under precarious conditions. This mixed evidence supports a lower acceleration score despite persistent harm. Regional conflict movements can still rise, and falling headcounts do not necessarily establish safe, durable recovery.

displacement.interdependence.source: IDMC, Global Report on Internal Displacement 2026
displacement.interdependence.note: IDMC documents displacement linked to both conflict and disasters, with different regional trajectories. These drivers connect housing, health, livelihoods and public-service capacity, supporting strong cross-sector coupling. Movement counts can include repeated displacement of the same person; the score judges linked systems rather than adding incompatible population totals.

displacement.irreversibility.source: UNHCR South Africa, World Refugee Day 2026: solidarity and solutions
displacement.irreversibility.note: UNHCR reports extensive protracted exile, demonstrating that displacement can persist and disrupt education, livelihoods and community continuity. This supports a moderate persistence judgment. Safe return, resettlement and local integration remain viable recovery pathways, so the range does not assume that displacement or its consequences are universally permanent.

displacement.gov_failure.source: UNRIC, July 2026 library newsletter: Global Trends, Forced Displacement in 2025
displacement.gov_failure.note: The UN's account of returns occurring under pressure or to precarious conditions indicates a gap between reduced displacement counts and durable protection. The central judgment reflects risks of inadequate reintegration and assistance. Outcomes depend on host-country inclusion, security and resources, so governance failure is plausible rather than certain.

displacement.growth_rate.source: UNRIC, July 2026 library newsletter: Global Trends, Forced Displacement in 2025
displacement.growth_rate.note: The UN summary reports falling global forced displacement in 2025. displacement.threshold.source: IDMC, Global Report on Internal Displacement 2026

economic.scale.source: IMF, Global Financial Stability Report April 2026: Global Financial Markets Confront the War in the Middle East and Amplification Risks
economic.scale.note: The IMF identifies several channels by which financial stress could spread through sovereign bonds, nonbanks and emerging-market capital flows. Such propagation can affect production, employment and public finances globally. The central score reflects potential systemic magnitude, while orderly market functioning and contained channels justify a substantial lower uncertainty bound.

economic.urgency.source: IMF, World Economic Outlook Update July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
economic.urgency.note: The IMF's July 2026 outlook describes uneven resilience, stalled disinflation and continuing conflict and repricing risks. These conditions warrant current policy attention, but its baseline still projects positive global growth. The urgency score therefore concerns exposure to shocks and limited policy room, not an asserted ongoing worldwide economic collapse.

economic.acceleration.source: IMF, World Economic Outlook Update July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
economic.acceleration.note: The July IMF outlook describes risks as more balanced than in April, even while adverse conflict and financial scenarios remain. This mixed picture warrants moderate, uncertain worsening rather than maximum acceleration. Forecast revisions and regional differences are not a directly observed annual growth series for systemic fragility.

economic.interdependence.source: IMF, Global Financial Stability Report April 2026: Global Financial Markets Confront the War in the Middle East and Amplification Risks
economic.interdependence.note: The IMF traces propagation through sovereign funding, banks, leveraged nonbanks, exchange rates and capital flows. These connect financial stress to many other threats and justify a high coupling judgment. The range allows monetary, fiscal and regulatory responses to interrupt cascades; interconnectedness also supplies financing and risk-sharing benefits during normal conditions.

economic.irreversibility.source: OECD, Supply Chain Resilience Review: Navigating Risks
economic.irreversibility.note: OECD scenarios show that disruptive relocalization can reduce output without consistently improving stability. Sustained trade and investment losses may create persistent damage, but economic networks can adapt and productive capacity can recover. The score therefore represents partial persistence; the scenario estimates are not observed permanent losses or inevitable future outcomes.

economic.gov_failure.source: IMF, World Economic Outlook Update July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
economic.gov_failure.note: The IMF calls for price stability, rebuilt fiscal space and greater adaptability while describing divergent national exposures. Meeting these goals simultaneously can be politically and institutionally difficult. The central score reflects that implementation challenge, with uncertainty recognizing functioning policy tools and the absence of an inevitable synchronized governance failure.

economic.growth_rate.source: IMF, World Economic Outlook Update July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
economic.growth_rate.note: The IMF July outlook combines continuing expansion with conflict exposure and repricing risks, providing no direct annual systemic-fragility series. epistemic.scale.source: Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: Overview and key findings
epistemic.scale.note: The Reuters Institute survey finds low news trust across many markets, supporting concern about the information environment at substantial scale. The score maps possible consequences for shared evidence and public decisions. Trust is an attitude rather than a measure of factual accuracy, and surveyed online populations are not a census of humanity.

epistemic.urgency.source: Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: Overview and key findings
epistemic.urgency.note: News trust declined significantly in 29 of 48 Reuters Institute survey markets in 2026. This supports a present need to strengthen reliable information and accountability. The central judgment remains below extreme because survey distrust can have legitimate causes and does not establish that people cannot obtain trustworthy information.

epistemic.acceleration.source: Reuters Institute, Digital News Report 2026: Overview and key findings
epistemic.acceleration.note: The Reuters Institute reports news trust falling from 40% to 37%, while news avoidance remained flat at 42%. These mixed indicators support material but uncertain worsening. The range reflects market variation and measurement limits; a change in trust cannot be equated with the growth rate of misinformation or societal irrationality.

epistemic.interdependence.source: Lorenz-Spreen et al., A systematic review of worldwide causal and correlational evidence on digital media and democracy, Nature Human Behaviour 7, 74-101 (2023)
epistemic.interdependence.note: Lorenz-Spreen and colleagues find links between digital media, political trust, participation and polarization across 496 studies. This supports coupling between information systems and governance, with plausible implications for collective responses to other threats. The mapping is inferential, and heterogeneous causal and correlational evidence prevents assigning a universal amplification coefficient.

epistemic.irreversibility.source: Lorenz-Spreen et al., A systematic review of worldwide causal and correlational evidence on digital media and democracy, Nature Human Behaviour 7, 74-101 (2023)
epistemic.irreversibility.note: The systematic review documents politically consequential media associations but also beneficial participation and information effects. This mixed evidence supports a recoverable, moderately persistent problem rather than irreversible epistemic failure. The numeric range reflects uncertainty about rebuilding trust, changing platform incentives and improving information practices; it is not a measured recovery time.

epistemic.gov_failure.source: V-Dem Institute, Democracy Report 2026: Unraveling the Democratic Era?
epistemic.gov_failure.note: V-Dem documents censorship and pressure on freedom of expression, identifying institutional obstacles to open scrutiny. These provide an anchor for concern about inadequate protection of information integrity. The score also permits functioning independent institutions; it does not imply that centralized censorship or uniform state control would remedy epistemic risk.

The wide range reflects uncertainty about societal adaptation and avoids interpreting either low survey trust or social-media use alone as a destabilization threshold.

fragmentation_gov.scale.source: United Nations Security Council, Highlights of Security Council Practice 2025
fragmentation_gov.scale.note: UN Security Council records show continuing decisions alongside unresolved disputes and veto use. The score concerns broad loss of coordination; Council voting is a partial institutional indicator and cannot measure all global governance.

fragmentation_gov.urgency.source: WTO, Large increase in new tariffs but also measures to ease global trade, annual monitoring report
fragmentation_gov.urgency.note: WTO monitoring documents sharply expanded tariff coverage while members still facilitate trade and pursue dialogue. The combination supports current action to preserve cooperation and manage disputes. The urgency range acknowledges functioning institutional channels and reversibility of policies; trade friction is evidence of strain rather than proof of comprehensive governance collapse.

fragmentation_gov.acceleration.source: United Nations Security Council, Highlights of Security Council Practice 2025
fragmentation_gov.acceleration.note: The Security Council reports fewer vetoes in 2025 than in 2024, while unanimous resolution adoption decreased from 65% to 61%. Decade totals indicate longer-term friction, but small annual counts and agenda selection preclude treating veto growth as a stable global trend.

fragmentation_gov.interdependence.source: IMF, Global Financial Stability Report April 2026: Global Financial Markets Confront the War in the Middle East and Amplification Risks
fragmentation_gov.interdependence.note: The IMF describes financial vulnerabilities amplified by geopolitical shocks and cross-border capital movements. This anchors the inference that impaired cooperation can weaken containment across debt, economic and security systems. The very high coupling score expresses the governance function across threats; it is not a measured correlation or independently estimated causal multiplier.

fragmentation_gov.irreversibility.source: United Nations Security Council, Highlights of Security Council Practice 2025
fragmentation_gov.irreversibility.note: Security Council activity continued in 2025 despite disagreement, showing that coordination capacity is impaired but still present. Lost trust and abandoned arrangements may take years to rebuild, supporting moderate persistence. Institutional cooperation can resume after political changes, so the range remains below irreversible physical-damage anchors.

fragmentation_gov.gov_failure.source: United Nations Security Council, Highlights of Security Council Practice 2025

The 8.1 model value is relatively low because governance supports containment of many other threats. No source measures this numerical boundary; the wide interval represents uncertainty in its cascade consequences.

geopolitics.scale.source: Uppsala University/UCDP, Record number of conflicts between states
geopolitics.scale.note: UCDP records 65 state-based conflicts in 2025, including eight interstate conflicts. The breadth and potential for escalation support high systemic magnitude through direct harm and spillovers. Conflict counts differ in severity and cannot be added as equivalent risks; the range allows substantial regional containment alongside worse escalation pathways.

geopolitics.urgency.source: Uppsala University/UCDP, Record number of conflicts between states
geopolitics.urgency.note: UCDP documents about 244600 deaths from organized violence in 2025 and several active interstate conflicts. Ongoing lethal harm and escalation exposure warrant high present-decade priority. The ordinal score is not a forecast of a world war; event estimates and the distribution of violence remain uncertain.

geopolitics.acceleration.source: SIPRI, Global military spending rise continues as European and Asian expenditures surge
geopolitics.acceleration.note: SIPRI estimates world military expenditure grew 2.9% in real terms in 2025, substantially slower than 9.7% in 2024, with divergent regional trends. The score reflects continued pressure without claiming accelerating spending growth. Spending can provide deterrence as well as conflict capability, which broadens uncertainty in the risk mapping.

geopolitics.interdependence.source: IMF, World Economic Outlook Update July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
geopolitics.interdependence.note: The IMF July outlook links the war shock to energy-import costs and uneven economic performance. This demonstrates a pathway from geopolitical conflict into prices, financing and supply systems. The high coupling judgment concerns transmission potential; the scale of spillovers depends on conflict geography, duration and policy responses.

geopolitics.irreversibility.source: Uppsala University/UCDP, Record number of conflicts between states
geopolitics.irreversibility.note: UCDP documents major lethal violence, establishing irreversible loss of life and persistent social harm. Infrastructure, livelihoods and relations may also recover after peace, so system-level irreversibility is not maximal. The range separates enduring consequences of war from a claim that every affected society permanently loses its capacity to function.

geopolitics.gov_failure.source: United Nations Security Council, Highlights of Security Council Practice 2025
geopolitics.gov_failure.note: UN Security Council records show both continued decisions and blocked proposals affecting major conflicts. This anchors substantial concern about diplomacy and enforcement under rivalry. The range allows successful bargaining and de-escalation; institutional disagreement is a partial measure, not an empirical probability that all conflict-management mechanisms will fail.

geopolitics.growth_rate.source: SIPRI, Global military spending rise continues as European and Asian expenditures surge
geopolitics.growth_rate.note: SIPRI reports 2.9% real growth in world military expenditure in 2025, slower than the revised 9.7% for 2024. The published inflation-adjusted annual change supplies the raw central proxy. Conversion produces a moderate effective rate; spending is not proportional to conflict probability and can also support deterrence, motivating wide bounds.

geopolitics.threshold.source: Uppsala University/UCDP, Record number of conflicts between states
geopolitics.threshold.note: UCDP's conflict evidence supports an 8.3 model anchor for multiple major conflicts causing persistent global security and economic cascades. This is not UCDP's empirical battle-death definition of armed conflict. The comparatively low anchor reflects escalation and cross-system spillovers; the bounds express uncertainty about containment and conflict geography.
geopolitics.threshold.model_anchor_note: Analyst-defined normalized model anchor. The linked evidence supports a failure pathway, not a measured numerical tipping point; mu and bounds are epistemic calibration judgments.

minerals.scale.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Executive summary
minerals.scale.note: IEA identifies concentrated mineral inputs that can disrupt several high-value industries. This supports major cross-sector economic consequences with a 3.5 center. The range recognizes strategic bottlenecks but also substitution, inventories and diversification; it does not equate production temporarily exposed to disruption with realized economic losses.

minerals.urgency.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Executive summary
minerals.urgency.note: IEA reports that export controls have already produced downstream disruptions while investment declined in 2025. Present dependence and slow capacity expansion justify urgency of 3.9. Available buffers and new projects permit a lower-risk case, and conditional future restrictions are not treated as already fully implemented.

minerals.acceleration.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Market overview
minerals.acceleration.note: IEA estimates recent energy-mineral demand growth near 10% annually, with much faster lithium demand and slower base-metal growth. This supports strong worsening exposure, centered at 3.8. The measure reflects demand growth, not mathematically established acceleration or automatic growth of scarcity when supply also expands.

minerals.interdependence.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Executive summary
minerals.interdependence.note: IEA describes mineral dependencies across energy, electronics, transport, aerospace and defence, compounded by trade restrictions. These shared chokepoints support 4.3 for systemic coupling. The interval allows different substitution possibilities and strategic buffers; small market size alone neither establishes nor excludes large downstream consequences.

minerals.irreversibility.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Executive summary
minerals.irreversibility.note: IEA identifies diversification, stockpiles and recycling as ways to reduce supply vulnerability. This keeps the central irreversibility score at 2.8 despite costly capacity rebuilding and long investment lead times. It evaluates supply-system recovery, with mining's local environmental damage represented as an additional uncertainty rather than universal permanent scarcity.

minerals.gov_failure.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Executive summary
minerals.gov_failure.note: IEA finds growing export restrictions and gaps between public funding commitments and disbursement. These barriers support 3.6 for inadequate coordination and execution. Active diversification programmes and modestly improving supply prospects temper the assessment; policy difficulty is not assigned a direct numerical probability of failure.

minerals.growth_rate.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Market overview
minerals.growth_rate.note: IEA reports recent energy-mineral demand growth near 10% annually. The raw center is 0.10 with analyst bounds 0.04-0.20 for basket and continuation uncertainty. Demand is a pressure proxy rather than measured scarcity growth; calibration prevents faster individual materials from automatically dominating the systemic model.

minerals.threshold.source: IEA, Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026: Executive summary
minerals.threshold.note: IEA's bottleneck evidence anchors a relatively high model threshold of 9.0: shortages become globally destabilizing when inventories, substitution and diversification fail across several essential sectors. The interval reflects uneven criticality. It is an analyst dashboard anchor, not a reserve-depletion year, price boundary or measured industrial collapse threshold.

nuclear.scale.source: Xia et al., Global food insecurity and famine from reduced crop, marine fishery and livestock production due to climate disruption from nuclear war soot injection, Nature Food 3, 586-596
nuclear.scale.note: Xia and colleagues model severe global food losses under nuclear-war soot scenarios, including potential famine deaths exceeding five billion in the large US-Russia case. This supports near-extreme potential magnitude. The estimate is conditional on war, soot injection and food-system assumptions and is neither an observed outcome nor an occurrence probability.

nuclear.urgency.source: SIPRI, Increasing focus on nuclear weapons amid heightened escalation risks, Yearbook 2026
nuclear.urgency.note: SIPRI estimates 2100-2200 deployed warheads on high operational alert in January 2026 and describes heightened escalation risks. These conditions support urgent prevention and crisis management now. The score does not infer that launch or war is imminent; deterrence, decision processes and incomplete public information create broad uncertainty.

nuclear.acceleration.source: SIPRI, Increasing focus on nuclear weapons amid heightened escalation risks, Yearbook 2026
nuclear.acceleration.note: SIPRI reports continued modernization by all nine nuclear-armed states and deployment of new systems by most during 2025. This supports meaningful capability-related worsening, but warhead totals alone show neither exponential risk growth nor uniform trends. The ordinal range captures uncertainty about qualitative modernization, posture and deterrence effects.

nuclear.interdependence.source: Xia et al., Global food insecurity and famine from reduced crop, marine fishery and livestock production due to climate disruption from nuclear war soot injection, Nature Food 3, 586-596
nuclear.interdependence.note: The Xia study links nuclear conflict to atmospheric soot, climate disruption and global food production, demonstrating a plausible multi-sector cascade beyond targeted countries. This supports very high interdependence. Results depend on scenario assumptions and response options; the score concerns propagation conditional on war rather than the probability of initiating it.

nuclear.irreversibility.source: Xia et al., Global food insecurity and famine from reduced crop, marine fishery and livestock production due to climate disruption from nuclear war soot injection, Nature Food 3, 586-596
nuclear.irreversibility.note: The modeled nuclear-war pathways include widespread mortality and prolonged food disruption. Loss of life is irreversible and large-scale reconstruction can be severely constrained, supporting a very high persistence judgment. Physical climate anomalies are not permanent in every scenario; the score does not claim that all nuclear effects or all affected ecosystems are irreversible.

nuclear.gov_failure.source: SIPRI, Increasing focus on nuclear weapons amid heightened escalation risks, Yearbook 2026
nuclear.gov_failure.note: SIPRI identifies deteriorating arms control, heightened geopolitical tension and greater reliance on nuclear weapons. These conditions justify high concern about prevention and escalation management. Governance failure remains uncertain because deterrence and command safeguards still operate; public stockpile data cannot identify a numerical probability of their breakdown.

nuclear.growth_rate.note: Reported military-stockpile estimates increased from 9614 to 9745, about 1.36%. SIPRI attributes much of the Russian increase to reassessment. This is an estimate-change proxy, not identified physical growth or nuclear-war probability. The 0-4% raw range is judgmental.

The Xia scenarios support this pathway but do not measure an Apocalypse Clock threshold. Relative placement is below slowly accumulating institutional threats because propagation may be rapid and losses difficult to reverse.

oceans.scale.source: FAO, State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2026: official findings
oceans.scale.note: FAO's 2026 report shows the food and livelihood importance of aquatic systems and substantial marine production. This anchors 4.2 for potential harm from major marine degradation. Reported dietary dependence also includes inland waters and aquaculture, so it cannot be assigned wholly to ocean collapse.

oceans.urgency.source: WMO, Earth's climate swings increasingly out of balance
oceans.urgency.note: WMO reports another ocean-heat record and widespread marine heatwaves in 2025. Ongoing exposure supports high current-decade priority, centered at 4.4. The interval allows local ecological resilience and effective management; marine heatwave exposure does not imply equivalent mortality or irreversible loss everywhere.

oceans.acceleration.source: WMO, Earth's climate swings increasingly out of balance
oceans.acceleration.note: WMO finds ocean warming during 2005-2025 exceeded twice the rate during 1960-2005. This provides stronger acceleration evidence than a record level alone, supporting 4.1. Ocean degradation has several drivers, however, and this thermal comparison cannot establish identical acceleration in fisheries, oxygen or acidity.

oceans.interdependence.source: FAO, State of World Fisheries and Aquaculture 2026: official findings
oceans.interdependence.note: FAO connects aquatic food systems with nutrition, livelihoods, trade, climate and geopolitical shocks. The resulting multiple-sector dependencies support coupling of 4.5. Some evidence combines marine, freshwater and farmed production; the score therefore reflects plausible ocean-mediated pathways rather than assigning every aquatic dependency to the sea.

oceans.irreversibility.source: WMO, Earth's climate swings increasingly out of balance
oceans.irreversibility.note: WMO describes ocean warming and deep-ocean pH changes as effectively irreversible for centuries to millennia. These physical commitments justify a 4.6 recovery-difficulty score. The lower bound acknowledges that fisheries and habitats can recover under management even while the ocean's accumulated heat burden persists.

oceans.gov_failure.source: FAO, Review of the state of world marine fishery resources 2025: official findings
oceans.gov_failure.note: FAO's expanded stock assessment finds large differences between effective management regions and areas with capacity and data gaps. A 3.7 center recognizes substantial institutional shortfalls alongside demonstrated recovery. The enlarged assessment sample cannot be treated as a direct worsening time series or proof that all marine governance fails.

oceans.growth_rate.source: WMO, Earth's climate swings increasingly out of balance
oceans.growth_rate.note: WMO's record ocean heat anchors a selected composite-pressure rate of 0.018 per year, with 0.006-0.040 bounds. This is therefore explicit model judgment, with management and biological responses widening uncertainty around continued degradation.

pandemics.scale.source: WHO, 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021
pandemics.scale.note: WHO estimated about 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the 2020-2021 pandemic, including direct and indirect effects. This historical consequence anchor supports severe global potential at 4.3. The score is a present model judgment across future pathogens, with a range for transmissibility, severity and response capacity.

pandemics.urgency.source: WHO, Six years after COVID-19's global alarm: Is the world better prepared for the next pandemic?
pandemics.urgency.note: WHO's February 2026 assessment reports improved preparedness but fragile, uneven gains and funding pressure. A 4.0 score reflects the present need to sustain response capacity before another emergency. The interval credits faster recent containment while acknowledging that readiness varies substantially across countries and pathogen types.

pandemics.acceleration.source: WHO, Six years after COVID-19's global alarm: Is the world better prepared for the next pandemic?
pandemics.acceleration.note: WHO reports both strengthened surveillance and more effective recent outbreak containment, alongside pressures on preparedness. These mixed signals justify a moderate 2.8 acceleration score. No comparable global series establishes a current pandemic-frequency increase; more detected outbreaks alone would not distinguish changing hazard from improved ascertainment.

pandemics.interdependence.source: WHO, 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021
pandemics.interdependence.note: WHO's excess-mortality assessment includes indirect pandemic effects, demonstrating consequences beyond recorded infections. A 4.4 model score reflects health-system disruption and broader societal transmission of shocks. Its range allows protective institutions and different response strategies; it does not count all excess deaths as directly caused by infection.

pandemics.irreversibility.source: WHO, 14.9 million excess deaths associated with the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020 and 2021
pandemics.irreversibility.note: WHO's historical mortality estimates establish permanent human loss. The 3.3 persistence judgment combines this with the fact that many population and service disruptions can recover after an emergency. The interval represents variation among pathogens and responses; historical deaths are not treated as a current annual growth indicator.

pandemics.gov_failure.source: WHO Member States continue negotiations on the Pathogen Access and Benefit Sharing Annex
pandemics.gov_failure.note: WHO's July 2026 update records progress but unfinished PABS negotiations, delaying the path to signature and ratification. A 3.7 score recognizes a material coordination gap while crediting ongoing cooperation. The range includes successful completion and improved preparedness; adoption of the agreement alone is not operational readiness.

pandemics.growth_rate.source: WHO, Six years after COVID-19's global alarm: Is the world better prepared for the next pandemic?
pandemics.growth_rate.note: WHO's 2026 preparedness assessment documents both improvement and fragility, without a comparable global pandemic-frequency trend. The raw 2% central pressure input and 0.1-5.5% range are analyst scenarios. Near-flat pressure is allowed; reported-outbreak growth is not treated as true frequency growth or as a forecast.

pandemics.threshold.source: WHO, Six years after COVID-19's global alarm: Is the world better prepared for the next pandemic?
pandemics.threshold.note: WHO's preparedness assessment anchors a critical state where transmission and simultaneous service needs exceed sustained response capacity across regions. The central 8.3 is a normalized scenario anchor, not a pathogen reproduction-number threshold. Its uncertainty includes countermeasures, public trust, health capacity and cross-border coordination.

pollution.scale.note: WHO attributes 4.2 million premature deaths in 2019 to ambient air pollution. This establishes large existing health harm and supports 4.0 for potential systemic magnitude across pollutants. The mortality estimate is historical and specific to air; it is not a measured total burden of all chemical pollution.

pollution.urgency.note: WHO describes a major preventable health burden and effective interventions across emitting sectors. These current, actionable harms support urgency of 4.2. Exposure improvements can deliver benefits, while uneven capacity and pollutant mixtures widen uncertainty; the score does not presume every environmental contaminant has an established comparable health effect.

pollution.acceleration.source: OECD, Plastics: production, use and policy outlook
pollution.acceleration.note: OECD documents sustained growth in plastic use and projects additional growth without stronger policies. This supports increasing production pressure, centered at 3.1, rather than proof of accelerating total toxic exposure. Historical material throughput, future scenarios and trends in regulated air pollutants are different quantities.

pollution.interdependence.source: OECD, Plastics: production, use and policy outlook
pollution.interdependence.note: OECD connects plastics with chemical exposure, climate emissions, waste systems and terrestrial and aquatic leakage. Multiple environmental and industrial pathways support coupling of 4.0. Plastics are only one component of pollution, and the interval allows mitigation or substitution to weaken links rather than assuming uniform amplification.

pollution.irreversibility.source: OECD, Plastics: production, use and policy outlook
pollution.irreversibility.note: OECD's leakage and lifecycle assessment anchors concern about accumulating dispersed plastic residues. A 3.8 center weights difficult recovery of environmental stocks, while allowing source controls and remediation. This is an analyst persistence judgment; reversible air-quality improvements and variable chemical lifetimes preclude treating all pollution as permanent.

pollution.gov_failure.source: UNEP, INC-5.2 plastics treaty negotiations: official session record
pollution.gov_failure.note: UNEP records that August 2025 plastics negotiations ended without consensus on a treaty text. This concrete coordination setback supports 4.0 for governance shortfall. Negotiations and existing national controls continue, so the event is an anchor for institutional difficulty rather than evidence that all pollution regulation has failed.

pollution.growth_rate.source: OECD, Plastics: production, use and policy outlook
pollution.growth_rate.note: OECD's 234-to-435 Mt plastic-use endpoints imply raw annual growth near 0.03149 for 2000-2020. Analyst bounds of 0.015-0.060 cover uncertain continuation and proxy mismatch. Plastic throughput does not directly measure leakage, toxic dose or trends across all pollutants, so systemic conversion remains a model assumption.

soils.scale.source: FAO, State of Food and Agriculture 2025 findings on land degradation
soils.scale.note: FAO estimates that 1.7 billion people live in areas with degradation-associated crop-yield losses. This supports major potential damage to agriculture and livelihoods, centered at 3.8. The estimate compares modeled natural baselines and current conditions; it does not measure an equivalent fraction of global food output already lost.

soils.urgency.source: FAO, State of Food and Agriculture 2025 findings on land degradation
soils.urgency.note: FAO links accumulated degradation to current productivity losses and identifies practicable restoration measures. Timely prevention and land management warrant a 3.7 priority score. Regional exposure and implementation capacity differ, and evidence of recoverable productivity keeps immediate urgency below the most rapidly unfolding global threats.

soils.acceleration.source: UNCCD Science-Policy Interface, global aridity trends assessment presented to COP16
soils.acceleration.note: UNCCD finds dryland expansion between two thirty-year climatologies, supporting a persistent worsening driver of soil stress. This establishes trend more directly than acceleration. A 2.8 center and wide bounds reflect nonlinear local responses while avoiding an unsupported claim that worldwide soil degradation accelerates uniformly.

soils.interdependence.source: UNCCD Science-Policy Interface, global aridity trends assessment presented to COP16
soils.interdependence.note: UNCCD connects increasing aridity with vegetation loss, soil fertility, water availability, wildfire and livelihoods. These coupled agricultural and ecological pathways support 4.2 for interdependence. Local management can interrupt feedbacks, and the score does not imply that aridity represents every mechanism of soil degradation.

soils.irreversibility.source: FAO, State of Food and Agriculture 2025 findings on land degradation
soils.irreversibility.note: FAO treats degradation as accumulated losses in ecosystem functions while identifying restoration opportunities. The 3.9 score weights enduring erosion and soil-function losses but allows recoverable carbon and management deficits. Recovery times and achievable restoration vary; the report does not directly quantify a global irreversibility index.

soils.gov_failure.source: FAO, State of Food and Agriculture 2025 findings on land degradation
soils.gov_failure.note: FAO finds that finance, incentives and farm structure affect adoption of sustainable land management. These persistent implementation barriers support a 3.6 governance-shortfall estimate. Available practices and tailored regulation create a credible lower-risk case, while unequal capacity and continued harmful land use motivate the upper bound.

soils.growth_rate.source: UNCCD Science-Policy Interface, global aridity trends assessment presented to COP16
soils.growth_rate.note: UNCCD's dryland share rises from 37.5% to 40.6% between climatologies separated by 30 years, yielding raw growth near 0.002651. Analyst bounds are 0.0007-0.008. This partial aridity driver supports growth below the usual 0.005 guideline; it is neither a global soil-loss rate nor a full degradation forecast.

soils.threshold.source: UNCCD Science-Policy Interface, global aridity trends assessment presented to COP16
soils.threshold.note: UNCCD's nonlinear ecosystem responses anchor a model threshold of 8.4 for extensive soil-function losses that exceed restoration and agricultural adaptation capacity. space.scale.source: ESA Space Environment Statistics, 31 July 2026 update
space.scale.note: ESA's July 2026 inventory reports about 16000 functioning satellites, demonstrating substantial exposed infrastructure. The 3.2 judgment represents major loss of orbital services rather than direct planetary destruction. The range reflects alternative terrestrial systems, geographic dependencies and the uneven consequences of losing particular orbital bands.

space.urgency.source: ESA Space Environment Report 2025, official overview
space.urgency.note: ESA describes increasingly necessary collision avoidance in busy orbits and incomplete removal of retired objects. A 3.8 score reflects operational pressure requiring action now. Improved disposal practices and variation among orbital regions support the lower bound; costly service disruption supports the upper range.

space.acceleration.source: ESA Space Environment Statistics, 31 July 2026 update
space.acceleration.note: ESA's July 2026 count is about 46770 tracked objects, above the roughly 40000 in its end-2024 overview. This inventory pressure supports 3.9 acceleration. Catalog growth includes active spacecraft and changing tracking coverage; it is neither a collision-rate estimate nor evidence that all orbits worsen equally.

space.interdependence.source: ESA Space Environment Report 2025, official overview
space.interdependence.note: ESA identifies orbital infrastructure supporting communication, navigation and climate observation. A 3.9 score reflects dependence of several terrestrial sectors on these services. Redundancy and alternative technologies keep the central judgment below maximal coupling; severe simultaneous disruption of multiple services remains an uncertain upper-tail scenario.

space.irreversibility.source: ESA Space Environment Report 2025, official overview
space.irreversibility.note: ESA explains that debris fragmentation can sustain long-lived damage in some orbital regions. This supports 3.8 for persistence, while natural decay and active removal make outcomes strongly orbit-dependent. The interval avoids treating the loss of one altitude band as irreversible loss of all space access.

space.gov_failure.source: ESA Space Environment Report 2025, official overview
space.gov_failure.note: ESA reports improving mitigation compliance and more controlled re-entries, alongside continued debris growth. These mixed outcomes anchor governance risk at 3.4. The lower bound credits demonstrated progress; the upper bound reflects gaps in global coordination and remediation, rather than assuming that standards have had no effect.

space.growth_rate.source: ESA Space Environment Statistics, 31 July 2026 update
space.growth_rate.note: ESA's 2025 overview gives about 40000 tracked objects; the 31 July 2026 update gives about 46770. A 19-month interval is assumed from the overview's end-2024 data cutoff, not an explicitly dated first count. This approximate inventory-pressure proxy is not collision frequency; the 3-22% raw range is judgmental.

space.threshold.source: ESA Space Environment Report 2025, official overview
space.threshold.note: ESA's orbit-specific cascade discussion anchors a critical state where debris persistence and service disruption exceed effective coordination and recovery. The 8.5 threshold is a model convention, not an estimated Kessler-syndrome boundary. The interval reflects orbital altitude, debris distribution, redundancy and uncertain future remediation.
space.threshold.model_anchor_note: Analytical scenario anchor on the model's 0-10 scale; not an observed tipping point, probability, forecast, or empirical calibration.

supply.scale.source: OECD, Supply Chain Resilience Review: Navigating Risks
supply.scale.note: OECD scenarios show substantial trade and output losses when production is broadly relocalized, supporting potentially severe disruption of essential supply networks. The score judges systemic consequences across food, energy and industry. Those scenario losses are not observed damage, and diversification or substitution can markedly reduce exposure.

supply.urgency.source: IMF, World Economic Outlook Update July 2026: Global Economy in Crosscurrents of War and Technology
supply.urgency.note: The IMF July 2026 outlook describes war-related pressure on energy importers, connecting current geopolitical events with supply costs. This supports urgent preparedness and adaptable sourcing. The range allows successful rerouting and adjustment; the central score does not imply a universal shortage or that all trade networks are failing.

supply.acceleration.source: WTO, Large increase in new tariffs but also measures to ease global trade, annual monitoring report
supply.acceleration.note: WTO monitoring shows a marked expansion of imports affected by accumulated tariffs and similar measures in 2025, alongside increased trade facilitation. This warrants substantial worsening of policy pressure. Tariffs are not equivalent to physical supply outages, and policy reversals, exemptions and supplier substitution create a wide mapping uncertainty.

supply.interdependence.source: OECD, Supply Chain Resilience Review: Navigating Risks
supply.interdependence.note: The OECD review examines trade dependencies and the costs of relocalization across production networks. Essential inputs can transmit disruptions among energy, industry and wider economic activity, supporting a very high coupling judgment. Network diversity can also distribute risk; the range allows differences in concentration, substitutability and inventory buffers.

supply.irreversibility.source: OECD, Supply Chain Resilience Review: Navigating Risks
supply.irreversibility.note: OECD emphasizes adaptable and diversified supply chains and finds that relocalization does not reliably improve resilience. Disruptions can create lasting investment and capability losses, yet routes, contracts and production often adjust. The moderate irreversibility score reflects this recoverability and does not treat a temporary logistical interruption as permanent damage.

supply.gov_failure.source: WTO, Large increase in new tariffs but also measures to ease global trade, annual monitoring report
supply.gov_failure.note: WTO records extensive new restrictions but also trade-facilitating measures and continued dialogue. This mixed evidence supports a substantial, non-extreme risk of inadequate coordination. The range reflects policy uncertainty and competing national objectives while acknowledging that cooperative mechanisms remain active and many restrictions can be reversed.

supply.growth_rate.source: WTO, Large increase in new tariffs but also measures to ease global trade, annual monitoring report
supply.growth_rate.note: WTO reports accumulated tariffs and similar measures affecting 19.7% of world imports versus 12.6% a year earlier, about 56.3% relative exposure growth. The calibrated central and upper rates hit the 0.04 safety cap. This is trade-policy coverage, not observed shortage growth, and facilitation, adaptation and denominator changes limit extrapolation.
supply.growth_rate.calibration_note: mu/lo/hi already store calibrated annual effective systemic risk-growth and must not be converted again. Apply min(log1p(raw)*0.25, 0.04); multiplier and cap are retained model conventions, not fitted empirical coefficients. Raw range is judgmental epistemic uncertainty.

supply.threshold.source: OECD, Supply Chain Resilience Review: Navigating Risks
supply.threshold.note: The OECD's production-network scenarios anchor an 8.5 model threshold for sustained interruption of several essential supply systems after substitution and rerouting fail. No empirical universal supply-chain threshold exists. Placement reflects strong coupling together with demonstrated adaptability; bounds describe uncertainty in this abstract model convention rather than measured shortage severity.
supply.threshold.model_anchor_note: Analyst-defined normalized model anchor. The linked evidence supports a failure pathway, not a measured numerical tipping point; mu and bounds are epistemic calibration judgments.

water.scale.source: UNESCO/UN-Water, World Water Development Report 2025: Facts and figures
water.scale.note: UNESCO reports severe seasonal water scarcity affecting approximately half the population, with agriculture dominating withdrawals. The 4.0 score reflects broad potential consequences for food, livelihoods and services. Seasonal exposure is not continuous deprivation, and geographic concentration and adaptive infrastructure widen the plausible severity range.

water.urgency.source: UNESCO/UN-Water, World Water Development Report 2026: Water for all people
water.urgency.note: UNESCO's 2026 assessment documents large daily water-collection burdens and unequal access, reinforcing immediate action needs. A central 4.2 combines persistent service deficits with scarcity exposure. Gendered burdens indicate present welfare losses but cannot alone determine a global destabilization probability or physical scarcity trend.

water.acceleration.source: Jasechko et al. (2024), Rapid groundwater decline and some cases of recovery in aquifers globally, Nature
water.acceleration.note: Jasechko and colleagues find accelerating groundwater declines in many monitored aquifers, alongside deceleration and recovery elsewhere. This mixed evidence supports 3.0 rather than universal rapid acceleration. The monitoring sample is not globally random, and groundwater-level change is not directly equivalent to water-storage or population-exposure growth.

water.interdependence.source: UNESCO/UN-Water, World Water Development Report 2025: Facts and figures
water.interdependence.note: UNESCO identifies agriculture as the largest water user and links mountain flows to irrigation and energy. Water therefore couples essential production with climate and ecosystem pressures, supporting 4.5. The range allows trade, efficiency and infrastructure to buffer local shortages before they become wider cascades.

water.irreversibility.source: Jasechko et al. (2024), Rapid groundwater decline and some cases of recovery in aquifers globally, Nature
water.irreversibility.note: The groundwater study documents serious depletion but also recoveries following policy changes, recharge and surface-water transfers. A 3.5 center reflects difficult, often slow recovery without assuming all losses are permanent. Hydrogeology, continued abstraction and ecosystem damage determine whether a depleted system can actually recover.

water.gov_failure.source: UNESCO/UN-Water, World Water Development Report 2025: Facts and figures
water.gov_failure.note: UNESCO reports that only 43 of 153 countries sharing transboundary waters cover at least 90% with operational cooperation arrangements. This incomplete coordination supports a substantial governance gap. Existing agreements and local management successes justify 3.7 rather than extreme failure across all basins.

water.growth_rate.source: UNESCO/UN-Water, World Water Development Report 2025: Facts and figures
water.growth_rate.note: UNESCO reports 14% growth in freshwater withdrawals during 2000-2021, giving approximately 0.006259 annual fractional growth. Analyst raw bounds of 0.002-0.015 allow uncertain persistence and scarcity coupling. Withdrawal growth is an indirect demand-pressure surrogate; it does not measure annual growth in people experiencing scarcity.
water.growth_rate.calibration_note: mu/lo/hi already contain min(log1p(raw) * 0.9, 0.035), using raw lo/mu/hi 0.002/0.006259/0.015; do not convert again. Multiplier and cap are retained model conventions, not empirically estimated causal factors. Raw bounds are analyst plausibility ranges, not confidence intervals. No lower-rate floor was needed. Active growth_kind=freshwater_withdrawal_pressure_growth. The raw indicator is freshwater withdrawals, not scarcity-exposed population.

water.threshold.source: UNESCO/UN-Water, World Water Development Report 2025: Facts and figures
water.threshold.note: UNESCO's food-water dependence anchors an analyst threshold of 8.1 for sustained shortages spreading beyond individual basins into multiple essential sectors. Storage, substitution and trade make the onset uncertain. The values represent normalized dashboard destabilization, not an empirical water-stress percentage or universal hydrological tipping point.
water.threshold.model_anchor_note: Analyst-chosen normalized destabilization anchor. The cited source motivates the relevant system dependencies but does not estimate this threshold or its bounds; these values are not measured physical tipping points.
